'''''Pinus parviflora''''', also known as '''Japanese white pine''',<ref name="iucn status 11 November 2021"/> is a [[pine]] in the [[Pinus classification|white pine]] group, ''[[Pinus]]'' subgenus ''[[Strobus]]'', native to Japan.

==Description==
It is a [[pinophyta|coniferous]] [[evergreen]] tree, growing to 15–25 m (rarely to 30 m) in height, forming a wide, dense, conical crown. The [[leaf|leaves]] are needle-like, in bundles of five, with a length of 3–7 cm. The [[conifer cone|cones]] are 4–8 cm long, with broad, rounded scales; the [[seed]]s are 7–10 mm long, with a vestigial 3–10 mm wing.<ref name="Farjon">{{cite book | last=Farjon | first=Aljos | title=Pines | publisher=Brill | publication-place=Leiden [etc.] | date=2005 | isbn=90-04-13916-8 | page=153 }}</ref><ref name="GD">{{cite web | title=''Pinus parviflora'' (ゴヨウマツ) description | website=The Gymnosperm Database | date=2025-02-22 | url=https://www.conifers.org/pi/Pinus_parviflora.php | access-date=2025-10-10}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Two [[variety (botany)|varieties]] are usually accepted; var. ''parviflora'' in southern Japan, and var. ''pentaphylla'' (Mayr) A.Henry in northern Japan.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web | title=Pinus parviflora Siebold & Zucc. | website=Plants of the World Online | date=2021-06-13 | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:263192-1 | access-date=2025-10-09}}</ref> The second variety was first described as a separate species ''Pinus pentaphylla'' by [[Heinrich Mayr]] in 1890, but in reducing it to the rank of variety in 1910, [[Augustine Henry]] pointed out that the differences cited by Mayr between the two were minimal and inconsistent, with much overlap.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Elwes | first1=Henry John | last2=Henry | first2=Augustine | last3=Henry | first3=Augustine | title=The trees of Great Britain & Ireland / by Henry John Elwes and Augustine Henry. | publisher=Priv. print. | publication-place=Edinburgh | year=1906 | doi=10.5962/bhl.title.17123 | doi-access=free | url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/itempdf/68650 | access-date=2025-10-10 | pages=1033–1035}}</ref>

At higher altitudes in northern Japan, it can occur with the related high altutude species ''[[Pinus pumila]]'', and sometimes produces [[hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] with it; these are known as ''[[Pinus × hakkodensis]]'' Makino, named after the [[Hakkōda Mountains]] where it was first found.<ref name="GD"/>

The Latin [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''parviflora'' means "with small flowers".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book | last=Harrison |first=Lorraine | title=RHS Latin for Gardeners | year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley | location=United Kingdom | isbn=978-1-84533-731-5 }}</ref>

==Uses==
It is a popular tree for [[bonsai]], and is also grown as an ornamental tree in parks and gardens. The [[cultivar]]s 'Adcock's Dwarf' and 'Bonnie Bergman'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/67902/i-Pinus-parviflora-i-Bonnie-Bergman/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Pinus parviflora'' 'Bonnie Bergman' | access-date = 2 May 2018}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Pinus parviflora'' 'Adcock's Dwarf'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/77345/Pinus-parviflora-Adcock-s-Dwarf/Details | access-date = 6 February 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 78 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 30 April 2018}}</ref>
